new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record. The only bearing content is group-level (MANGBUTU-EFE tonal, ~3 levels; no uniform stress pattern found); it supplies no word-stress placement for Mangbutu, so nothing placement-bearing should be staged from this work. Consistent with Vorbichler's 1967 BSOAS review already read held by the project (three tonemes in Mangbutu-Efe; his penultimate-stress remark concerns Balese, not Mangbutu).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The chapter treats MANGBUTU-EFE (with MAMVU as main exponent; MANGBUTU proper cited only for a few morphological forms) as tonal: apparently three tone levels, tone classes in nouns and verbs not yet worked out. On stress it gives a placement only for MANGBETU (Larochette: penultimate tendency), MORU (initial) and MA'DI (final) and states that no uniform stress pattern has been found in the other language groups, which include MANGBUTU-EFE. No Mangbutu-specific (or Mamvu-specific) stress placement is given anywhere the full-text search could reach.
new_statements.exceptions: none for Mangbutu; the group-level remark is explicitly negative ('No such uniformity of stress pattern.. has been found in the other Language Groups')
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan describe the MANGBUTU-EFE group with MAMVU (mamv1243) as main exponent; MANGBUTU proper (mang1396) appears only in a few cited forms (omo mangbutu 'I am a Mangbutu', tribal-name morphology). Any prosodic statement in the chapter is therefore group-level, not a description of Mangbutu itself.

sources.note: p. 452 'Tone and stress': three distinctive tonemes established for Mangbutu-Efe (via Balese, then Mamvu); in Balese a long (not virtually disyllabic) syllable 'always indicates a stress on the penultimate of a word, word complex, or syntactic unit'.
